## Market-implied points

A spread $s$ (home's line) and a total $T$ imply points for each team:

$$
\text{home} = \frac{T}{2} - \frac{s}{2}, \qquad \text{away} = \frac{T}{2} + \frac{s}{2}.
$$

Those implied points are the benchmark the model's per-team predictions are compared to
(@tbl-test).

## Edges and results

From the two team predictions, $\widehat{m} = \widehat{\text{home}} - \widehat{\text{away}}$
and $\widehat{T} = \widehat{\text{home}} + \widehat{\text{away}}$. Against a line:

$$
\text{spread edge} = \widehat{m} + s, \qquad \text{total edge} = \widehat{T} - T.
$$

A positive spread edge means the model likes home; a positive total edge means the over.

## Break-even and ROI at −110

Risking 110 to win 100 pays $100/110$ per unit risked. Break-even solves
$p \cdot \tfrac{100}{110} = (1 - p)$:

$$
p^\ast = \frac{110}{210} \approx 52.38\%.
$$

ROI per unit risked is $p\,(1 + \tfrac{100}{110}) - 1$. Pushes return the stake and are
excluded from win rates.

## Closing line value (CLV)

CLV measures how far the line moved *toward* a pick between when it was taken (the
opener) and kickoff (the close):

$$
\text{CLV}_{\text{total}} = \operatorname{sign}(\text{edge}) \cdot (T_{\text{close}} - T_{\text{open}}).
$$

Taking over 50 and seeing it close at 52 is +2: the market later agreed. Positive CLV is
the most stable early sign of real edge, because it doesn't depend on the noisy outcome
of the game. Across the held-out seasons, the model's picks against the opener had
**positive CLV every year, growing with the size of the edge** (about +0.3 to +1.0
points in 2025).

## The pre-registered paper rules

Both rules were fixed on 2026-09-23, before any 2026 prediction was graded. They're
tracked on paper only.

| Rule | Bet | Evidence when registered |
|---|---|---|
| **A · `edge4`** | The model's side when \|model total − opening total\| ≥ 4 | 57.8% (2024, n = 213) and 55.2% (2025, n = 201); the only rule above break-even in both held-out years, within about 1 SE; threshold chosen after looking |
| **B · `shootout_under`** | The under when the ratings' expected total exceeds 63.5 | 55–60% under in every season 2021–2025; 56.4% vs the opener pooled over 2021–2025 (n = 509) |

: Paper-trading rules. {#tbl-rules}

The rules can disagree. On day one, Ole Miss at Florida was an **over** for A (model
66.8 vs 59.2) and an **under** for B (expected total 68.5). Each rule is graded on its
own, and the conflict itself points at the next piece of work (@sec-roadmap).

**Decision rule for real money, set in advance:** at least one full season of paper
results, a win rate above 52.4%, and positive CLV.

## The weekly pipeline

`scripts/predict_week.py` runs the whole week in about a minute:

1. Refresh the current season: ESPN scores plus CFBD lines and advanced stats (about 3
   CFBD calls).
2. Rebuild the feature table.
3. Refit the final model on every completed game since 2016.
4. Predict both teams' points (and every half and quarter) for the next slate.
5. Compute edges against the opening lines, and append the rule A and B picks to
   `paper_trading/2026_bets.csv`. A (game, rule) pair already logged keeps its first
   pick.

`scripts/grade_paper.py` grades finished games (win/loss/push at the opening total,
units at −110, CLV) by rule and by week.

A **GitHub Action** (`.github/workflows/weekly.yml`) runs both every Wednesday at 13:00
UTC (9:00 ET, before the Thursday games) and commits the picks and results. That makes
git's timestamps the proof that every pick came before its game. A clean-machine
simulation reproduced exactly the same picks as the local run.
